blocks: This study aims to explore the applicable selectivity of size and color of the Apple Snails by the Snail Kite. Also, possible specific plant-snail association is examined. It was expected that the Snail Kite would be selective for larger and lighter colored snails because they are more easily located and provide maximum caloric return. Furthermore, it was predicted that the Apple Snail would in fact show a specific plant association.

The study was conducted at the Palo Verde National Park between October 11 and October 14 of 2003 (wet season) in the freshwater marsh, where Pomacea flagellata are frequently preyed upon by Rostrhamus sociabilis. Palo Verde National Park lies in the Rio Tempisque lowlands in a tropical dry forest, covering an area of 13, 058 hectares.⁵ In this area, there is a defined dry season, January through March, as well as a wet season, June through December.

To evaluate size, a comparison was made between snail size and color by examining consumed snails and the live snail population. We identified nine perches of Snail Kites and gathered 400 snail shells from beneath these perches. The shells were collected by hand when floating or by using a net when they were on the marsh floor. These shells were then measured for shell length, shell width, operculum length, operculum width with Vernier calipers (precision ± 0.001m), and shade (light or dark using a color chart). To compare the general population of snails available to the Snail Kite, the live population of snails was sampled by gathering snails from randomly placed transects in the vicinity of the identified perches. Randomization was achieved by using a stopwatch to determine number of paces out from the shore that a transect should begin in the area of a known perch. One transect was 50m by 2m and nine transects were 25m by 2m because we found it to be more time efficient (the 50m by 2m transect is excluded in analysis due to disproportion). Only the live snails on the surface were collected, where surface is defined as all floating vegetation and open areas of water. Snails collected in the transects were then measured just as those collected from beneath the perches. To evaluate plant-snail associations, the dominant plant species in terms of highest percent coverage was recorded for every 10m² in each of the transects sampled for live snails.
Since the distribution of snail shell sizes between the transects was not normal, a Wilcoxon/Kruskal Wallis test was used to compare mean shell size collected

between transects and perches (it is important to note that operculum length and width were used in shell size comparisons because it was established as a more stable measurement for snail size). Then, a Chi Square analysis was done to determine Snail Kite preference for color of snail shell, where color is defined as light or dark. In addition, one way ANOVA analysis was performed on operculum size (operculum length by width) between perches to determine foraging differences between individuals within the Snail Kite population itself. Finally, the relation between operculum size and shell size was evaluated using regression analysis. In our second objective, we assessed the possibility of specific plant-snail association. As the transects were completed for the primary objective, the dominant vegetation for every 5 meters was observed and recorded as well as the number of snails collected. After establishing that there was a statistically significant difference in the number of snails collected between transects by using a Chi Square analysis, these observations of dominant vegetation were employed to relate snail density to vegetation type, thereby reflecting any specific plant-snail association. This analysis and all others were completed using the JMP 3.2 statistical analysis program (SAS Institute 1997).

The 400 snail shells collected from the perches were compared to the 313 live snails collected in the transects. Snail Kites were highly selective for larger snails present in the nine perches (Fig. 1), but were shown to have no preference for color of snail shell (Fig. 2). Also, snails in the live population showed no bias toward lighter or darker shell color (Fig. 2). Snail shell sizes differed significantly between perches (Figure 3), indicating distinct ownership of each perch. After the regression analysis (Fig. 4), operculum size (operculum length by width) was shown to be highly correlated with shell size (shell size by width). Finally, since there was a significant difference in the number of live snails collected in each transect (Fig. 5), these differences indicate discrepancies in the aquatic plant distribution in each transect, suggesting the existence of specific plant-snail relationships.
